commit.message:
feat(effects)!: emit, apply, and effects as the only replication mechanism (#2570)

* feat(effects): emit, apply, and the host wiring

What connects the v3 codec beneath this to the engine: a finished transaction
becomes records, records become graph mutations, and a payload reaches a
replica.

    v3/emit.rs       Pending -> Record, grouped by shape
    v3/apply.rs      Record -> Graph, with the schema verified before any row
    v3/format.rs     v3 as an `EffectsFormat`: a whole payload, sent and applied
    effects/mod.rs   EffectsBuffer, EffectsPayload, ReplicationSink
    effects/error.rs ApplyError
    src/commands/effect.rs, graph_core.rs, divergence_guard.rs

This is the only PR of the three that changes existing behaviour, which is
where review effort belongs. The codec beneath it adds files and touches
nothing; this one rewrites how a write replicates.

The seam is deliberate and narrow: the format says that the bytes are sent and
what they are, and the host says what sending means. `ReplicationSink` takes a
key and a payload — not a command and an argv — because this crate does not
know it is running inside Redis, and naming `GRAPH.EFFECT` here would have made
every future transport something that has to be spelled as a Redis command.

Notable behaviour, all of it covered:

  - a divergence is reported with the payload rendered *and* its raw bytes, so
    it can be compared against the origin's own record of what it sent
  - a record covering no entities is refused at the header, before any block:
    `count` sizes every block that follows, so one check keeps a zero-length
    parse path out of all of them
  - a label record stating no labels is not emitted — it is an instruction to
    do nothing, and a C replica refuses it, which is a forced-resync loop
  - an update to an entity the transaction deletes is not emitted either, while
    the query still reports the property as set: what the replica needs and
    what the query did are different questions

INDEX OPTIONS CROSS BOTH CONVERSIONS AS OPTIONS. `wire_index_options` no
longer materialises what the statement omitted and `index_options` no longer
fills it in on arrival, because an absent option is an instruction not to
touch that setting. `test_CRUD_replication` is what established this:

    Replica diverged from master applying GRAPH.EFFECT on graph 'replication':
    Can not override index configuration: Language is already set for label 'L'.

`index_options` also no longer matches strings or checks types — the block
arrives typed, so what used to be `map_to_index_options` on this side (look up
"dim", assert it is an integer, reject an unknown key) now happens on the
primary at parse time. A malformed option is a decode error on a payload
rather than an apply error on a graph.

Two narrowings on the way in are checked rather than cast, both proved by
breaking them:

  - `dimension` is `size_t` on the wire and `u32` here. `as u32` turns 2^32
    into 0 and indexes against it; it is now `try_from` and a refusal.
  - an unrecognised `simFunc` is refused, not read as L2. Choosing a metric on
    the replica's behalf builds an index that answers different queries from
    the primary's and never says so.

FOUR MERGED PRs WERE BEING REVERTED, and are not any more. The branch carried
older copies of five shared files, so its diff undid work that is on `main`:

    graph/src/graph/endpoint_index.rs             #2691  endpoint paging
    graph/src/runtime/functions/algo_procedures.rs #2686  LAGraph adjacency
    graph/src/runtime/vector_expr.rs              #2685  label-as-column
    graph/src/runtime/runtime.rs (label helpers)  #2685
    graph/src/runtime/ops/value_hash_join.rs      #2690  inline build slot
    tests/flow/test_hashjoin.py                   #2690
    tests/flow/test_multi_label.py                #2685

All restored from `main`. The flow count going 1478 -> 1480 is those two test
files coming back, and unit 342 -> 348 is the same for the Rust tests — which
is the check that the restore was real rather than textual.

Only `graph/src/planner/mod.rs`'s deletion stays: `expr_has_non_deterministic`
and its two helpers existed so v2 could decide whether a write was safe to
replicate as effects. v3 has no fallback to decide about, so they have no
caller left.

This commit no longer touches the codec beneath it either. `records.rs` keeps
its own `read_buffer` test helper instead of importing the one `test_aux.rs`
adds here — a one-line duplication is cheaper than a layer PR reaching up into
the layer above it.

flow 1480/1480, unit 348 pass (1 pre-existing GraphBLAS failure — a library
assertion this branch does not touch), clippy clean across the effects tree.

* docs(effects/v3): correct and cite the comments asserting what C does

Audited the verb-bearing comments in emit/apply/error against origin/master
rather than a local checkout, which was 26 commits stale.

One was false, in two places. `dimension` is not C's `size_t`: C types it
`uint32_t` (src/index/index_field.h:45), the same width this engine holds.
The `size_t` in that struct belongs to the next three fields, M /
efConstruction / efRuntime, which is the likely source of the misreading --
and is why those cast plainly while this one does not. The `u64` on the wire
is v3's own choice, because dimension is the one vector option with no absent
form. The checked narrowing stays: a u64 field can carry a dimension neither
engine can hold. Only the stated reason was wrong.

Two were imprecise. The relationship-type check is not what ApplyUpdateEdge
"opens with" -- it is the fourth validation, after the record is read; the
check itself and its log text match exactly. And the refusal to set an
index-level option twice is this engine's behaviour, not a universal one: C
emits one record per field and gets away with it by making that work
idempotent, as create_index_effect.c says of Index_SetLanguage and
Index_SetStopwords.

The rest were accurate and now cite a file. Two are worth keeping in view:
C's ADD_SCHEMA and ADD_ATTRIBUTE records carry no id at all, which is why its
reader cannot see an id mismatch; and C's AttributeSet really does carry no
ascending guarantee -- AttributeSet_Add appends and AttributeSet_Contains
scans linearly, under a standing TODO.

* test(replication): assert the replicated index OPTIONS, not just that they agree

test_CRUD_replication already created a fulltext index with
OPTIONS {language: 'german', stopwords: ['a', 'b']} and then compared
db.indexes() between master and replica. That comparison is symmetric: it
passes just as well when both sides lose the options, so it cannot see one
dropped on the way out or materialised into a default on the way in. Across
the whole flow suite 'german' appeared exactly once -- at the CREATE -- and
was never asserted.

Assert the stated values on the replica.

Confirmed it can fail rather than assuming it: with wire_index_options
emitting no language, the replica reports 'english' -- the default, not
absence -- and this fails with "'english' == 'german'" where the symmetric
comparison fails with an unreadable list diff. Restored, and green again.

* refactor(graph): validate the node id space a batch leaves behind

Two ad-hoc checks in the effects apply path stood in for a question the
graph cannot answer: a boundary frozen at buffer entry, and a running set of
the ids the buffer had created so far. Neither is the question. Whether the
ids a batch hands the graph describe a possible id space is, and nothing
could ask it.

`Graph` tracks node liveness with `node_count` and `deleted_nodes` and no
live set, so the only boundary it can offer is
`node_count + deleted_nodes.len()`. That is the boundary *if the id space is
dense*, and `max_node_id` is the same arithmetic -- so an assertion written
in terms of them checks one derivation of the state against another
derivation of the same state, and passes on a graph that is already wrong.

Density holds between batches, not within one. Records are ingested grouped
by shape rather than ordered by id, so a create of 500..600 may precede one
of 0..500; between them the graph holds 100 live nodes whose highest id is
599 and reports its boundary as 100.

`NodeIdSpace` holds the boundary as it stood before the batch and every id at
or above it the batch has ingested, which states the invariant directly:

    ingested == [ entry_bound, entry_bound + ingested.len() )

It lives beside the graph rather than in the effects module because that is
what it is about. Nothing in it knows about replication, buffers or a peer
engine, and it decides nothing while the batch runs -- `create_nodes` already
refuses an id that is live below the boundary -- so it records and then
judges rather than gating each step.

Two independent things break the invariant, so `verify` checks both, and
neither subsumes the other.

The shape of what arrived: ids at or above the boundary must fill the range
from it upward. An allocator hands out the lowest free id, so it cannot reach
an id without having handed out everything below -- a batch that leaves a
hole did not come from one. This is what catches a replica that has missed a
buffer: told to create 500..600 when its own boundary is 0, it would
otherwise accept an id space its master does not have and collide on its next
allocation. Written as `len - 1 == highest - entry_bound`, because both sides
are subtractions that cannot wrap where the `+ 1` form can.

That the graph counted it: the same id ingested twice moves `node_count`
twice while the set absorbs the duplicate, so the range still looks whole.
Comparing the graph's own boundary against `entry_bound + ingested.len()` is
the only place anything checks that counter against a value not derived from
it. The cost is that a duplicate is now reported at the end of the batch and
without naming the id -- naming it would need the set to remember how many
times each id arrived, or to shrink on delete, and a delete followed by a
recreate of the same id inside one batch is legitimate, so no record-level
check can tell the two apart.

`created_here` and `entry_unallocated` go, and with them the last caller of
`Graph::first_unallocated_node_id`, which is deleted: it was a derived
quantity that read as ground truth, and the one place the derivation is sound
now states its own assumption instead of implying it everywhere.

* docs(effects/v3): the applier calls it the created set, as the type does

Two comments in apply.rs still called it "the ingested set". `ingested` was the
field's name before the id-space naming pass renamed it to `created`, so both
referred to something that no longer exists under that name, in the file that
is the set's main consumer.

Found while checking a draft review reply that claims the vocabulary was
unified. It was, in id_space.rs; these two were the last of the old one, and
they sit outside that file, which is why the pass missed them.

* refactor(effects/v3): emit and apply follow the codec's one-variant-per-opcode

The codec split five flag-carrying Record variants into fifteen, one per
opcode, and made encode fallible. This is emit and apply catching up; the wire
is unchanged, so nothing here should alter what a replica receives.

The renames are mechanical. What is not:

`Record::Update` becoming UpdateNode/UpdateEdge removes a state rather than
renaming one. An edge update carried `labels` it could never fill and a node
update an `Option<u32>` type it could never have, so `checked_type_id` took an
Option purely to reject a case the wire could produce and the emitter never
did. It takes a `u32` now, and `ApplyError::MissingRelType` is gone with it --
not handled better, unrepresentable.

The same for `status` on a constraint and `options` on an index: a create
carries them and a drop has no field for them, so
`ApplyError::MissingConstraintStatus` and an `Option` unwrap both disappear
into the type.

`index_options` and `wire_index_options` mostly delete. The record holds
`TextIndexOptions` and `VectorIndexOptions` themselves now, so what was a
field-by-field copy is a choice of which half the field type calls for. That
copy was not neutral: it checked a `dimension` that no longer needs checking --
both sides hold a u64 -- and it narrowed `phonetic` through a `bool`, which was
the only narrow representation in the chain and silently rewrote any algorithm
other than Double Metaphone English.

Two unit tests went with the conversions they guarded. The dimension check has
nothing left to refuse. The unrecognised-similarity-function check moved *down*
into the codec, where an unknown discriminant is now a decode error on the
payload rather than an apply error on a graph -- earlier, and where it belongs.

On the fallible encode: no `.unwrap()` on any production path. An EncodeError
means the emitter built a record wrong, so it fails the write. `build` returns
`Result<u64, String>` up through EffectsBuffer to the commit op, which returns
it as a query error rather than panicking a server. The two closure-shaped call
sites needed a helper each, since `for_each_record` and `emit_schema_additions`
hand records to an `FnMut` that cannot return one; both stop at the first
refusal, because every later record would be written into a buffer that is
already not what the replica will be told it is.

Every record is also built before anything is written, so a refusal leaves the
buffer untouched rather than torn -- the property the codec's own conversion
missed until a test asserted the buffer was unchanged.

Verified: cargo test -p graph 364 passed 0 failed - flow test_replication 2/2,
test_effects 21/21, test_constraint 17/17, test_index_create 17/17 - fmt clean -
clippy clean, no warning in the effects tree or id_space.

* fix(effects): GRAPH.EFFECT creates a graph the way every other command does

From Copilot's review on #2570. Two of its three comments were real; this is
both of them.

**The key a new graph lands under.** `GRAPH.EFFECT` opened and created through
the key it was addressed with, where `GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT`,
`GRAPH.PROFILE` and `GRAPH.BULK` all create through `c_graph_name` /
`c_graph_key`. Those differ once a key holds a NUL, and the result was worse
than a naming inconsistency -- measured on a live server, before and after:

    before   key = a\0b   GRAPH.LIST = a
    after    key = a      GRAPH.LIST = a

So the graph was stored somewhere it did not claim to be: unreachable by the
name it advertises, and a later write to `a` builds a second graph beside it
that nothing reconciles. On the replication path, between a replica and the
master it is copying.

C does the same truncation here, checked rather than assumed. `cmd_effect.c`
calls `GraphContext_RetrieveOrForce(ctx, argv[1], false, true, &gc)` -- and the
header names those parameters `readOnly` and `shouldCreate`, so C creates too,
through `GraphContext_New(graph_name)` + `GraphContext_SetKey`
(`graphcontext_retrieve.c:67`), which is the asymmetry `c_graph_key` documents.
Reading `false` at the call site as "does not create" is the mistake this note
exists to stop the next person making.

The lookup keeps the full key bytes, which is C's asymmetry and was already
right.

**A docstring that outlived its function.** `take_effects_buffer` carried two
stacked doc comments, the older one saying `None` means verbatim replication --
the mechanism this PR removes -- directly above the new one saying there is no
such alternative any more. The stale half is gone.

Copilot's third comment, that `matches!(pairs.value(i), Value::Null)` cannot
compile against a `&Value`, is wrong: match ergonomics handle it, the pattern
appears four times, and the crate builds.

The regression test is proven rather than assumed. It failed against the
unfixed binary with exactly `['a\0b'] == ['a']` and passes against the fixed
one.

Verified: flow test_nul_bytes 22/22 (was 21) - test_effects 21/21 -
test_replication 2/2 - cargo test -p graph 364 passed 0 failed - fmt clean -
clippy clean, the one remaining warning being an 8-argument function present
unchanged on main.

* fix(effects): four findings from CodeRabbit's review of #2570

Each verified against the code before changing anything; one turned out to be
unreachable and is noted as such rather than left unexplained.

**A panic on the apply path.** `AddAttribute` registered a name and then read
its id back with `expect`. `AttrNameMap::insert` returns *without inserting*
once the dictionary is full -- `ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE` is reserved out of a `u16`,
so the cap is 65535 -- and it says nothing when it declines. Reading back then
gives `None`, and the `expect` took the replica down over a buffer its master
had applied without trouble. Now `ApplyError::AttributeLimitReached`, which is
a divergence: the master interned the name, so from that point the two
dictionaries disagree and every later bare attribute id means something
different on each side. The test fills the dictionary and fails with a panic at
that exact line when the `expect` is put back.

**A shape check that was skipped for empty attribute sets.** `CreateNode` and
`CreateEdge` ran `check_attr_shape` inside `if !attr_ids.is_empty()`, and with
no attributes that check is precisely what says `rows` must be empty too
(`rows.len() != ids.len() * 0`). `UpdateNode` has always checked
unconditionally, so one record shape reached the two paths differently. Hoisted
above the gate in both.

Unreachable from the wire, and worth saying so: the decoder builds `rows` as
`count x attr_ids.len()`, so a decoded record with no attributes has no values.
This closes it for records built in process, and removes the asymmetry.

**A settle that reported success after doing nothing.** `upgrade_to_write`
takes the per-graph lock but not `MvccGraph`'s write slot, so another writer can
hold it. That arm returned silently, which made `attempt_settle` answer `Ok(())`
and broke the retry loop as though the constraint had settled -- leaving it
UNDER CONSTRUCTION with nothing logged and nothing able to re-drive it, since
`GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE` answers "already exists". The closure now reports
whether it settled and a busy slot is `WriteAbort::WriteSlotBusy`, retried
alongside `ReplicaTrafficPaused` because both windows close on their own.

**A key rendered through a String before being replicated under.**
`settle_constraint` took `&str` and announced with `key.as_bytes()`. A Redis key
is binary -- `test_binary_key_name_scan_skip` keeps a graph under `\xc3\x28` --
so a non-UTF-8 key was announced under one holding U+FFFD instead. It takes
`&[u8]` now, the command path hands over `key_str.as_slice()` verbatim, and the
lossy rendering is used only for log lines.

The promotion path still reads `GRAPH_REGISTRY`, which is keyed by the Redis key
rendered lossily. That is exact for every UTF-8 key including one holding a NUL,
which round-trips; a genuinely non-UTF-8 key is the registry's limitation rather
than this path's, shared with telemetry, the RDB save and the virtual-key
builder. Documented at the call site rather than fixed here, because fixing it
means re-keying the registry module-wide.

Also removes `MissingRelType` and `MissingConstraintStatus`, which the previous
commit made unconstructible and left declared. The claim that they were gone is
true now.

Verified: cargo test -p graph 365 passed 0 failed - flow test_constraint 17/17,
test_nul_bytes 22/22, test_effects 21/21, test_replication 2/2,
test_index_create 17/17 - fmt clean - clippy clean.

* fix(constraint): a missing status skips the announcement, not the process

From @AviAvni's "what about the expect" on #2570, which had gone unanswered.

`find_status` was unwrapped with `expect("a create leaves its constraint in
place")`. The invariant holds -- the graph write lock has been held since
`create_constraint` stored it -- but the write has already committed by that
point, so a panic would take the server down over a bookkeeping surprise
instead of losing one announcement. That is the same trade the `Err` arm four
lines below already makes for a failed `build_constraint`, and it now makes it
the same way: log what happened, name the recovery, return the reply the
command would have returned anyway.

No test. The branch is unreachable by construction, which is why it was an
`expect` in the first place; what changed is the failure mode if it ever stops
being unreachable. The early return mirrors the function's own tail and sits
after the validation-thread spawn, so nothing else is skipped.

Verified: cargo test -p graph 365 passed 0 failed - flow test_constraint 17/17,
test_effects 21/21, test_replication 2/2 - fmt clean - clippy clean.

* refactor(constraint): intern the schema at the command, not inside create_constraint

@AviAvni's point on #2570, and he was right about the layering: the registration
does not belong inside `Graph::create_constraint`, which is a state mutation and
stores names rather than ids.

It cannot be deleted -- three consumers need the ids to exist and none of them
can create one. The RDB encoder takes `&self`; `build_constraint_buffer` runs
after the commit; C's `Constraint_New` takes `AttributeID *fields` outright. So
it has to happen on the write path. But `create_constraint` has exactly one
caller, and the other two constraint entry points do not need it:
`upsert_constraint_raw` runs behind `verify_schema`/`verify_attribute`, and
`add_constraint_raw` gets names that came out of the dictionary in the first
place. So the command is where it goes.

ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why it is a named function
with the reasoning attached rather than four inline lines.

*After* the create succeeds. `create_constraint` refuses a duplicate and a
UNIQUE with no supporting index; neither should leave a name interned. Rollback
would discard it anyway -- everything between `MvccGraph::write` and the commit
runs on the private COW version, and `rollback` only releases the write flag,
never publishing it -- but not interning on a refused create makes that
independent of the MVCC model instead of reliant on it. Pinned by test02.

*Before* the announcement and *after* the baseline. `SchemaBaseline::of` is
captured ahead of the mutation and the effect is a diff against it, so interning
before the baseline would hide exactly the entries that need announcing.

Two regression tests, and #2749 had none. Measured on `main` first to be sure
the case was real: `MANDATORY Q [z]` comes back as `MANDATORY Q [a]` after
DEBUG RELOAD, because `encode_constraint_block` resolves an unregistered
property with `position(..).unwrap_or(0)` and the decoder reads `attribute_names[0]`.
Both tests fail when the registration is removed -- test01 with exactly
`[['Q', ['a']]] == [['Q', ['z']]]`, which is the corruption itself.

Verified: cargo test -p graph 365 passed 0 failed - flow test_constraint 19/19
(was 17), test_effects 21/21, test_replication 2/2, test_nul_bytes 22/22,

* test(effects): the divergence report asserts through env, not through raise

@AviAvni on #2570. Six `raise AssertionError` / `raise RuntimeError` calls
become `env.assertContains` / `assertTrue` / `assertEqual`.

Not only style. RLTest records an env assertion and carries on; a bare raise
aborts the method and is reported as "Exception raised during test execution"
rather than as a failure, so every later check in the same test is lost and the
summary says nothing about which assertion went. The report has five
independent properties to check -- records, values, raw bytes, the truncation
limit, the resync -- and a raise on the first hides the other four.

Verified: 1/1.

* test(effects): a divergence-report test per record kind

@AviAvni on #2570: "test all kinds of divergence". The file covered
`CreateNode` -- what an empty graph's first write happens to emit. All fifteen
kinds now have a test each:

    AddLabel  AddRelType  AddAttribute
    CreateNode  CreateEdge  UpdateNode  UpdateEdge
    SetLabels  RemoveLabels  DeleteNode  DeleteEdge
    CreateIndex  DropIndex  CreateConstraint  DropConstraint

Each asserts the record is named *and* that its own fields survived into the
line -- `relation_id` and the endpoint columns for an edge, `status` for a
constraint create, the new value for an update. The name alone would pass a
rendering that dropped every field, and the fields are what someone matches a
log line against the query that ran on the master.

THREE THINGS THE WRITING TURNED UP:

The replica's log is cumulative across the class, so `_wait_for_log` matched a
report left by an earlier test and returned instantly -- every assertion after
that read the wrong payload, and the first version of this "passed" while
looking at the previous test's output. It takes a byte offset now, captured
before the write.

Deleting a node with no relationships emits `DeleteNode` and nothing else, so
`DeleteEdge` needs the doomed node to carry an edge for the delete to cascade.

The drops need a different collision entirely. A drop introduces no schema, so
the master's payload claims no id the replica could already hold and the
label-collision trick cannot fire on one. Dropping on the replica first is what
makes the master's drop unapplicable there.

Also drops `config_set("EFFECTS_THRESHOLD", 0)` and the comment justifying it.
v3 replicates every write as effects; the knob survives as a deprecated no-op,
stored and echoed back by GRAPH.CONFIG and never read for a decision, so setting
it only looked like it mattered.

Verified: 16/16 in 99s, and not vacuous -- with the record rendering stripped to
`record[N]`, test06 fails with "no CreateEdge record in" and passes restored.

* perf(effects): a cancelled node travels as ids, not as a node

@AviAvni on #2570: "no need labels/attrs in create and delete node for
cancelled".

The pair exists to move the replica's allocator over an id the master handed out
and then took back -- not to reproduce a node that did not survive its own
transaction. Carrying its labels and attributes had the replica build a node and
then immediately unbuild it: the create adds index documents, the delete a
record later removes them, and the net effect on the graph is the id space and
nothing besides.

`DeleteNode` never read them anyway. `apply` binds it as `labels: _`, so on that
half the list was already dead weight on the wire.

What goes with the content is the grouping. Shapes earn their grouping when the
content travels with them; with no content, every cancelled node in the buffer is
one record pair however many labels they had between them -- and the per-node
`find` over its attribute list, and the `Value` clone per cell, go too.

Verified: cargo test -p graph 365 passed 0 failed (the one flake is
`list_literals_parse_in_linear_time`, a timing test that passes alone in 0.04s) -
flow test_effects 21/21, test_replication 2/2, test_divergence_report 16/16 -
fmt clean - clippy clean.

* fix(effects): a cancelled edge leaves the same hole a cancelled node does

@AviAvni on #2570 asked "digest_cancelled_edges?" and he was right — there was
none, and the omission is not cosmetic.

`delete_pending_node` unwinds a node created in the same commit, and
`remove_pending_relationships_for_node` takes every relationship hanging off it
with it -- out of `created_rels_by_type`, out of its attrs, out of the deleted
set. The node was recorded in `cancelled_nodes` and became a create/delete pair;
its edges were recorded nowhere and became nothing. So the buffer for

    CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b), (c)-[:R]->(d) DELETE a

carried `CreateEdge{ids:[1]}` and never mentioned id 0.

That is refused, not tolerated. The two id spaces are the same machinery --
`reserve_relationships` mirrors `reserve_nodes`, `return_relationship_id`
mirrors `return_node_id` into a recycle bin, and `apply` runs
`IdSpace::verify` on both. Applying that buffer to a fresh graph gives

    IdsHaveAHole { kind: "relationship", entry_bound: 0, highest: 1, created: 1 }

-- the whole payload rejected, and a forced full resync every time an ordinary
query cancels an edge.

The two paths are now one `digest_cancelled`, because splitting them is what let
the second be forgotten. Order inside it is load-bearing and is why it cannot be
two independent functions: an edge's endpoints may themselves be cancelled, so
the nodes are created before the edges and deleted after them, mirroring
`digest_deleted_edges` running before `digest_deleted_nodes`.

`CancelledNode` collapses to a bare id -- once the pair stopped carrying content
its labels and attrs were dead, and clippy said so. `CancelledRelationship`
keeps its type and endpoints only because `CreateEdge` has no form without them.

ONE CASE THIS CANNOT CLOSE, stated where the code skips it: a type whose *every*
edge was cancelled is never registered on the master -- nothing of it reached
`create_relationships_bulk` -- so there is no id to state and no ADD_SCHEMA
announcing one. Inventing one would index the pair under a different type. Those
ids stay reserved on the master and unmentioned on the replica, which leaves the
two relationship bounds apart without a refusal. It needs a record shape this
format does not have.

Three tests, each failing with the edge half removed: the pair is emitted, the
nodes bracket the edges, and a replica applies the buffer instead of refusing it
with the error above.

Verified: cargo test -p graph 368 passed 0 failed - flow test_effects 21/21,
test_replication 2/2, test_divergence_report 16/16, test_constraint 19/19 - fmt
clean - clippy clean.

* test(effects): pin the one cancellation shape whose ordering is not obvious

Checking Avi's question the other way round — is there a site that should record
a cancelled relationship and does not — turned up no gap but one shape worth a
test.

`remove_pending_relationships_for_node` is the single choke point: all three
`return_relationship_id` callers go through it, so recording inside it covers
every path. But only *one* of those three cancels the node as well. The other
two delete a node that was already committed and cascade its pending edges away,
which means the endpoint is removed by `digest_deleted_nodes` — and that runs
*before* the cancelled block. So the `CreateEdge` names a node the replica has
just deleted.

Measured rather than assumed: it applies, and the resulting state is right.
`relationship_count` 0, `deleted_relationships` 1, the endpoint still deleted.
The pair nets out, and the only lasting effect is the id reaching the recycle
bin — which is the whole reason it is sent.

Pinned because it holds by tolerance rather than by construction: nothing stops
`create_relationships_bulk` from refusing a deleted endpoint one day, and the
two orderings this block has to satisfy point opposite ways — a cancelled node
endpoint wants the edge created *after* it, a committed deleted one wants it
*before*. The block cannot satisfy both, so the test says which way it went and
what makes that safe.

* feat(effects): emit, apply, and the host wiring

What connects the v3 codec beneath this to the engine: a finished transaction
becomes records, records become graph mutations, and a payload reaches a
replica.

    v3/emit.rs       Pending -> Record, grouped by shape
    v3/apply.rs      Record -> Graph, with the schema verified before any row
    v3/format.rs     v3 as an `EffectsFormat`: a whole payload, sent and applied
    effects/mod.rs   EffectsBuffer, EffectsPayload, ReplicationSink
    effects/error.rs ApplyError
    src/commands/effect.rs, graph_core.rs, divergence_guard.rs

This is the only PR of the three that changes existing behaviour, which is
where review effort belongs. The codec beneath it adds files and touches
nothing; this one rewrites how a write replicates.

The seam is deliberate and narrow: the format says that the bytes are sent and
what they are, and the host says what sending means. `ReplicationSink` takes a
key and a payload — not a command and an argv — because this crate does not
know it is running inside Redis, and naming `GRAPH.EFFECT` here would have made
every future transport something that has to be spelled as a Redis command.

Notable behaviour, all of it covered:

  - a divergence is reported with the payload rendered *and* its raw bytes, so
    it can be compared against the origin's own record of what it sent
  - a record covering no entities is refused at the header, before any block:
    `count` sizes every block that follows, so one check keeps a zero-length
    parse path out of all of them
  - a label record stating no labels is not emitted — it is an instruction to
    do nothing, and a C replica refuses it, which is a forced-resync loop
  - an update to an entity the transaction deletes is not emitted either, while
    the query still reports the property as set: what the replica needs and
    what the query did are different questions

INDEX OPTIONS CROSS BOTH CONVERSIONS AS OPTIONS. `wire_index_options` no
longer materialises what the statement omitted and `index_options` no longer
fills it in on arrival, because an absent option is an instruction not to
touch that setting. `test_CRUD_replication` is what established this:

    Replica diverged from master applying GRAPH.EFFECT on graph 'replication':
    Can not override index configuration: Language is already set for label 'L'.

`index_options` also no longer matches strings or checks types — the block
arrives typed, so what used to be `map_to_index_options` on this side (look up
"dim", assert it is an integer, reject an unknown key) now happens on the
primary at parse time. A malformed option is a decode error on a payload
rather than an apply error on a graph.

Two narrowings on the way in are checked rather than cast, both proved by
breaking them:

  - `dimension` is `size_t` on the wire and `u32` here. `as u32` turns 2^32
    into 0 and indexes against it; it is now `try_from` and a refusal.
  - an unrecognised `simFunc` is refused, not read as L2. Choosing a metric on
    the replica's behalf builds an index that answers different queries from
    the primary's and never says so.

test_CRUD_replication already created a fulltext index with

db.indexes() between master and replica. That comparison is symmetric: it
passes just as well when both sides lose the options, so it cannot see one
dropped on the way out or materialised into a default on the way in. Across
the whole flow suite 'german' appeared exactly once -- at the CREATE -- and
was never asserted.

emitting no language, the replica reports 'english' -- the default, not

* refactor(graph): validate the node id space a batch leaves behind

Two ad-hoc checks in the effects apply path stood in for a question the
graph cannot answer: a boundary frozen at buffer entry, and a running set of
the ids the buffer had created so far. Neither is the question. Whether the
ids a batch hands the graph describe a possible id space is, and nothing
could ask it.

`Graph` tracks node liveness with `node_count` and `deleted_nodes` and no
live set, so the only boundary it can offer is
`node_count + deleted_nodes.len()`. That is the boundary *if the id space is
dense*, and `max_node_id` is the same arithmetic -- so an assertion written
in terms of them checks one derivation of the state against another
derivation of the same state, and passes on a graph that is already wrong.

Density holds between batches, not within one. Records are ingested grouped
by shape rather than ordered by id, so a create of 500..600 may precede one
of 0..500; between them the graph holds 100 live nodes whose highest id is
599 and reports its boundary as 100.

`NodeIdSpace` holds the boundary as it stood before the batch and every id at
or above it the batch has ingested, which states the invariant directly:

    ingested == [ entry_bound, entry_bound + ingested.len() )

It lives beside the graph rather than in the effects module because that is
what it is about. Nothing in it knows about replication, buffers or a peer
engine, and it decides nothing while the batch runs -- `create_nodes` already
refuses an id that is live below the boundary -- so it records and then
judges rather than gating each step.

Two independent things break the invariant, so `verify` checks both, and
neither subsumes the other.

The shape of what arrived: ids at or above the boundary must fill the range
from it upward. An allocator hands out the lowest free id, so it cannot reach
an id without having handed out everything below -- a batch that leaves a
hole did not come from one. This is what catches a replica that has missed a
buffer: told to create 500..600 when its own boundary is 0, it would
otherwise accept an id space its master does not have and collide on its next
allocation. Written as `len - 1 == highest - entry_bound`, because both sides
are subtractions that cannot wrap where the `+ 1` form can.

That the graph counted it: the same id ingested twice moves `node_count`
twice while the set absorbs the duplicate, so the range still looks whole.
Comparing the graph's own boundary against `entry_bound + ingested.len()` is
the only place anything checks that counter against a value not derived from
it. The cost is that a duplicate is now reported at the end of the batch and
without naming the id -- naming it would need the set to remember how many
times each id arrived, or to shrink on delete, and a delete followed by a
recreate of the same id inside one batch is legitimate, so no record-level
check can tell the two apart.

`created_here` and `entry_unallocated` go, and with them the last caller of
`Graph::first_unallocated_node_id`, which is deleted: it was a derived
quantity that read as ground truth, and the one place the derivation is sound
now states its own assumption instead of implying it everywhere.

* docs(effects/v3): the applier calls it the created set, as the type does

Two comments in apply.rs still called it "the ingested set". `ingested` was the
field's name before the id-space naming pass renamed it to `created`, so both
referred to something that no longer exists under that name, in the file that
is the set's main consumer.

Found while checking a draft review reply that claims the vocabulary was
unified. It was, in id_space.rs; these two were the last of the old one, and
they sit outside that file, which is why the pass missed them.

* refactor(effects/v3): emit and apply follow the codec's one-variant-per-opcode

The codec split five flag-carrying Record variants into fifteen, one per
opcode, and made encode fallible. This is emit and apply catching up; the wire
is unchanged, so nothing here should alter what a replica receives.

The renames are mechanical. What is not:

`Record::Update` becoming UpdateNode/UpdateEdge removes a state rather than
renaming one. An edge update carried `labels` it could never fill and a node
update an `Option<u32>` type it could never have, so `checked_type_id` took an
Option purely to reject a case the wire could produce and the emitter never
did. It takes a `u32` now, and `ApplyError::MissingRelType` is gone with it --
not handled better, unrepresentable.

The same for `status` on a constraint and `options` on an index: a create
carries them and a drop has no field for them, so
`ApplyError::MissingConstraintStatus` and an `Option` unwrap both disappear
into the type.

`index_options` and `wire_index_options` mostly delete. The record holds
`TextIndexOptions` and `VectorIndexOptions` themselves now, so what was a
field-by-field copy is a choice of which half the field type calls for. That
copy was not neutral: it checked a `dimension` that no longer needs checking --
both sides hold a u64 -- and it narrowed `phonetic` through a `bool`, which was
the only narrow representation in the chain and silently rewrote any algorithm
other than Double Metaphone English.

Two unit tests went with the conversions they guarded. The dimension check has
nothing left to refuse. The unrecognised-similarity-function check moved *down*
into the codec, where an unknown discriminant is now a decode error on the
payload rather than an apply error on a graph -- earlier, and where it belongs.

On the fallible encode: no `.unwrap()` on any production path. An EncodeError
means the emitter built a record wrong, so it fails the write. `build` returns
`Result<u64, String>` up through EffectsBuffer to the commit op, which returns
it as a query error rather than panicking a server. The two closure-shaped call
sites needed a helper each, since `for_each_record` and `emit_schema_additions`
hand records to an `FnMut` that cannot return one; both stop at the first
refusal, because every later record would be written into a buffer that is
already not what the replica will be told it is.

Every record is also built before anything is written, so a refusal leaves the
buffer untouched rather than torn -- the property the codec's own conversion
missed until a test asserted the buffer was unchanged.

* fix(effects): GRAPH.EFFECT creates a graph the way every other command does

From Copilot's review on #2570. Two of its three comments were real; this is
both of them.

**The key a new graph lands under.** `GRAPH.EFFECT` opened and created through
the key it was addressed with, where `GRAPH.QUERY`, `GRAPH.CONSTRAINT`,
`GRAPH.PROFILE` and `GRAPH.BULK` all create through `c_graph_name` /
`c_graph_key`. Those differ once a key holds a NUL, and the result was worse
than a naming inconsistency -- measured on a live server, before and after:

    before   key = a\0b   GRAPH.LIST = a
    after    key = a      GRAPH.LIST = a

So the graph was stored somewhere it did not claim to be: unreachable by the
name it advertises, and a later write to `a` builds a second graph beside it
that nothing reconciles. On the replication path, between a replica and the
master it is copying.

C does the same truncation here, checked rather than assumed. `cmd_effect.c`
calls `GraphContext_RetrieveOrForce(ctx, argv[1], false, true, &gc)` -- and the
header names those parameters `readOnly` and `shouldCreate`, so C creates too,
through `GraphContext_New(graph_name)` + `GraphContext_SetKey`
(`graphcontext_retrieve.c:67`), which is the asymmetry `c_graph_key` documents.
Reading `false` at the call site as "does not create" is the mistake this note
exists to stop the next person making.

The lookup keeps the full key bytes, which is C's asymmetry and was already
right.

**A docstring that outlived its function.** `take_effects_buffer` carried two
stacked doc comments, the older one saying `None` means verbatim replication --
the mechanism this PR removes -- directly above the new one saying there is no
such alternative any more. The stale half is gone.

Copilot's third comment, that `matches!(pairs.value(i), Value::Null)` cannot

* fix(effects): four findings from CodeRabbit's review of #2570

Each verified against the code before changing anything; one turned out to be
unreachable and is noted as such rather than left unexplained.

**A panic on the apply path.** `AddAttribute` registered a name and then read
its id back with `expect`. `AttrNameMap::insert` returns *without inserting*
once the dictionary is full -- `ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE` is reserved out of a `u16`,
so the cap is 65535 -- and it says nothing when it declines. Reading back then
gives `None`, and the `expect` took the replica down over a buffer its master
had applied without trouble. Now `ApplyError::AttributeLimitReached`, which is
a divergence: the master interned the name, so from that point the two
dictionaries disagree and every later bare attribute id means something
different on each side. The test fills the dictionary and fails with a panic at
that exact line when the `expect` is put back.

**A shape check that was skipped for empty attribute sets.** `CreateNode` and
`CreateEdge` ran `check_attr_shape` inside `if !attr_ids.is_empty()`, and with
no attributes that check is precisely what says `rows` must be empty too
(`rows.len() != ids.len() * 0`). `UpdateNode` has always checked
unconditionally, so one record shape reached the two paths differently. Hoisted
above the gate in both.

Unreachable from the wire, and worth saying so: the decoder builds `rows` as
`count x attr_ids.len()`, so a decoded record with no attributes has no values.
This closes it for records built in process, and removes the asymmetry.

**A settle that reported success after doing nothing.** `upgrade_to_write`
takes the per-graph lock but not `MvccGraph`'s write slot, so another writer can
hold it. That arm returned silently, which made `attempt_settle` answer `Ok(())`
and broke the retry loop as though the constraint had settled -- leaving it
UNDER CONSTRUCTION with nothing logged and nothing able to re-drive it, since
`GRAPH.CONSTRAINT CREATE` answers "already exists". The closure now reports
whether it settled and a busy slot is `WriteAbort::WriteSlotBusy`, retried
alongside `ReplicaTrafficPaused` because both windows close on their own.

**A key rendered through a String before being replicated under.**
`settle_constraint` took `&str` and announced with `key.as_bytes()`. A Redis key
is binary -- `test_binary_key_name_scan_skip` keeps a graph under `\xc3\x28` --
so a non-UTF-8 key was announced under one holding U+FFFD instead. It takes
`&[u8]` now, the command path hands over `key_str.as_slice()` verbatim, and the
lossy rendering is used only for log lines.

The promotion path still reads `GRAPH_REGISTRY`, which is keyed by the Redis key
rendered lossily. That is exact for every UTF-8 key including one holding a NUL,
which round-trips; a genuinely non-UTF-8 key is the registry's limitation rather
than this path's, shared with telemetry, the RDB save and the virtual-key
builder. Documented at the call site rather than fixed here, because fixing it
means re-keying the registry module-wide.

Also removes `MissingRelType` and `MissingConstraintStatus`, which the previous
commit made unconstructible and left declared. The claim that they were gone is
true now.

`upsert_constraint_raw` runs behind `verify_schema`/`verify_attribute`, and
`add_constraint_raw` gets names that came out of the dictionary in the first
place. So the command is where it goes.

ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, which is why it is a named function
with the reasoning attached rather than four inline lines.

*After* the create succeeds. `create_constraint` refuses a duplicate and a

never publishing it -- but not interning on a refused create makes that
independent of the MVCC model instead of reliant on it. Pinned by test02.

*Before* the announcement and *after* the baseline. `SchemaBaseline::of` is
captured ahead of the mutation and the effect is a diff against it, so interning
before the baseline would hide exactly the entries that need announcing.

and then took back -- not to reproduce a node that did not survive its own
transaction. Carrying its labels and attributes had the replica build a node and
then immediately unbuild it: the create adds index documents, the delete a
record later removes them, and the net effect on the graph is the id space and

`DeleteNode` never read them anyway. `apply` binds it as `labels: _`, so on that
half the list was already dead weight on the wire.

content travels with them; with no content, every cancelled node in the buffer is

* fix(effects): a cancelled edge leaves the same hole a cancelled node does

@AviAvni on #2570 asked "digest_cancelled_edges?" and he was right — there was
none, and the omission is not cosmetic.

`delete_pending_node` unwinds a node created in the same commit, and
`remove_pending_relationships_for_node` takes every relationship hanging off it
with it -- out of `created_rels_by_type`, out of its attrs, out of the deleted
set. The node was recorded in `cancelled_nodes` and became a create/delete pair;
its edges were recorded nowhere and became nothing. So the buffer for

    CREATE (a)-[:R]->(b), (c)-[:R]->(d) DELETE a

carried `CreateEdge{ids:[1]}` and never mentioned id 0.

That is refused, not tolerated. The two id spaces are the same machinery --
`reserve_relationships` mirrors `reserve_nodes`, `return_relationship_id`
mirrors `return_node_id` into a recycle bin, and `apply` runs
`IdSpace::verify` on both. Applying that buffer to a fresh graph gives

    IdsHaveAHole { kind: "relationship", entry_bound: 0, highest: 1, created: 1 }

-- the whole payload rejected, and a forced full resync every time an ordinary
query cancels an edge.

+//! What happened, as the emitter is told it — before any version has a say.
+//!
+//! These describe a mutation, not a wire: a constraint's type and status, an
+//! index's fields and options, how many schema entries existed beforehand.
+//! Nothing here is a width, a tag or an opcode. Which is why they sit beside
+//! the format traits rather than under a version — the *encoding* of an
+//! announced index is v3's, the announced index itself is not, and a v4 will
+//! encode these same three types differently rather than needing three of its
+//! own.
+//!
+//! They were under `v3::emit`, which meant a caller describing a constraint had
+//! to name a wire version to do it.
+
+use std::sync::Arc;
+
+use crate::{
+    entity_type::EntityType,
+    graph::constraint::{ConstraintStatus, ConstraintType},
+    graph::graph::Graph,
+    index::IndexType,
+    runtime::value::Value,
+};
+
+/// How many schemas and attributes a graph held before some mutation.
+///
+/// Records carry bare ids, so a buffer is only meaningful to a replica that
+/// numbers its dictionaries the same way. Anything registered after this
+/// baseline has to be announced in the same buffer, ahead of the records that
+/// reference it.
+pub struct SchemaBaseline {
+    pub labels: usize,
+    pub types: usize,
+    pub attrs: usize,
+}
+
+impl SchemaBaseline {
+    /// The counts as they stand now.
+    #[must_use]
+    pub fn of(g: &Graph) -> Self {
+        Self {
+            labels: g.get_labels().len(),
+            types: g.get_types().len(),
+            attrs: g.get_node_attribute_names().len(),
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+/// One constraint statement, and the status this node reached on it.
+///
+/// Announced twice when validation runs in the background — once UNDER
+/// CONSTRUCTION, once with whatever it settled on — so the same constraint
+/// arrives with a different `status`. The apply side upserts, so the second
+/// announcement converges on the first rather than duplicating it.
+pub struct AnnouncedConstraint<'a> {
+    pub ct: ConstraintType,
+    pub entity_type: EntityType,
+    /// The status this node reached, and `None` for a drop — which carries no
+    /// status field at all.
+    pub status: Option<ConstraintStatus>,
+    pub label: &'a str,
+    pub properties: &'a [Arc<String>],
+}
+
+/// One index DDL statement, as the runtime evaluated it.
+///
+/// `options` is the raw `OPTIONS {...}` map rather than the parsed
+/// `IndexOptions`: v2 could not encode it at all and forced the whole statement
+/// to replicate as a verbatim query, whereas v3 puts the map on the wire so the
+/// replica rebuilds exactly what the master built instead of approximating it.
+pub struct AnnouncedIndex<'a> {
+    pub entity_type: EntityType,
+    pub index_type: &'a IndexType,
+    pub label: &'a str,
+    pub fields: &'a [Arc<String>],
+    pub options: Option<&'a Value>,
+}

+/// A payload being built, in the version this build writes.
+///
+/// The write-side counterpart to [`EffectsPayload`], which is about a payload

+//! Turning a finished query into the payload it replicates.
+//!
+//! The buffer itself is built during execution — `CommitOp` for data records,
+//! [`crate::runtime::index_ddl`] for index DDL — and this is where it is handed
+//! over, or found to be empty.
+//!
+//! It lives in this crate rather than beside the command handlers because the
+//! buffer and the counters belong to `Runtime`. The host owns transport alone:
+//! when a payload is sent, under which key, over which context. What the bytes
+//! are is [`crate::effects::EffectsFormat`]'s.
+
+use crate::effects::EffectsBuffer;
+use crate::runtime::runtime::Runtime;
+
+/// The payload a finished write should replicate, or `None` when it produced
+/// nothing.
+///
+/// The buffer itself was built in `CommitOp`, before `Pending` was cleared.
+///
+/// There is no query-replay alternative any more: a write either ships as
+/// effects or is not replicated at all. That removes the size heuristic this
+/// used to run — `EFFECTS_THRESHOLD` only ever chose between effects and
+/// replaying the query — and with it the possibility of the two engines
+/// disagreeing about which mechanism carried a given write.
+pub fn take_effects_buffer(runtime: &Runtime) -> Option<EffectsBuffer> {
+    let buf = runtime.effects_buffer.borrow_mut().take()?;
+    // A payload holding nothing but its header carries no records. How long a
+    // header is belongs to the format, not to this function.
+    (!buf.is_empty()).then_some(buf)
+}

+//! Applying a v3 effects payload on a replica.
+//!
+//! The v2 path decodes and applies in one pass, and has to reconstruct batches
+//! it never received: it accumulates runs of adjacent `DELETE_NODE` records
+//! because applying a node's edges one at a time made a replica ~40x slower than
+//! the master that produced the writes.
+//!
+//! v3 needs none of that. A record already covers every entity of its shape, so
+//! the buffer decodes to a list of records and each one applies as a single bulk
+//! operation. The look-ahead, the two pending batches and the flush-on-type-change
+//! logic all disappear.
+//!
+//! ## What this path verifies that v2 could not
+//!
+//! `ADD_SCHEMA` and `ADD_ATTRIBUTE` now carry the id the master assigned. The
+//! replica computes the id it *would* assign and rejects the whole buffer if they
+//! disagree. That check is the point of v3: every other record identifies labels,
+//! types and attributes by a bare id, and until now nothing established that the
+//! two engines had numbered them the same way.
+
+use super::records::IndexFieldOptions;
+use crate::{
+    effects::v3::{
+        AttrRef, INDEX_FLD_FULLTEXT, INDEX_FLD_VECTOR, Record, entity_tag, open_payload,
+    },
+    entity_type::EntityType,
+    graph::{
+        attribute_store::MAX_ATTRIBUTES,
+        graph::{Graph, NodeOpError, TypeId},
+        id_space::{IdSpace, IdSpaceError},
+    },
+    index::{IndexType, indexer::IndexOptions},
+    runtime::{pending::IndexDocs, value::Value},
+};
+// Not v3's: applying a payload can fail the same ways whatever version
+// wrote it, so the error lives beside `DecodeError`. Re-exported because
+// this is where callers have always found it.
+pub use crate::effects::error::{ApplyError, LocalName};
+use rustc_hash::FxHashMap;
+use std::sync::Arc;
+
+impl From<String> for ApplyError {
+    fn from(e: String) -> Self {
+        Self::Graph(e)
+    }
+}
+
+/// What accumulates across a buffer and is settled once, at the end.
+struct BufferOps {
+    /// The same type the write path collects into, rather than a second set of
+    /// four maps that has to agree with it by inspection.
+    docs: IndexDocs,
+    /// The node id space this buffer is building.
+    ///
+    /// Held here rather than on the graph because its lifetime is the buffer's,
+    /// and a buffer is a thing only this file knows about. What the graph does
+    /// know is how to maintain one: `create_nodes` and `delete_nodes` take it and
+    /// feed it themselves, so nothing here can create a node and forget to
+    /// account for it — and nothing can be handed a graph without saying what to
+    /// do about validation, because the argument is not optional to supply.
+    nodes: IdSpace,
+    /// And the relationship one. Same type, same checks — the id spaces are two
+    /// counted ranges with recycle bins, and nothing about the invariant differs.
+    edges: IdSpace,
+}
+
+/// Apply a whole `GRAPH.EFFECT` payload.
+///
+/// Every failure aborts the buffer rather than applying a prefix: effects are
+/// transactional, and a record that does not decode means the replica has
+/// diverged.
+pub fn apply_effects(
+    g: &mut Graph,
+    buf: &[u8],
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    // Decode one record, apply it, drop it. The alternative — decoding every
+    // record first — holds the whole buffer's worth of owned ids, labels and
+    // values before touching the graph, and walks that memory twice. Streaming
+    // keeps a record hot in cache between being decoded and being applied, and
+    // caps live decoded state at one record whatever the payload holds.
+    //
+    // A compressed payload still has to be inflated whole before any of it can
+    // be read; `open_payload` owns that plaintext and the records borrow from it.
+    let payload = open_payload(buf)?;
+
+    let mut ops = BufferOps {
+        docs: IndexDocs::default(),
+        nodes: IdSpace::at(g.node_id_bound()),
+        edges: IdSpace::at(g.relationship_id_bound()),
+    };
+
+    for record in payload.records() {
+        apply_record(g, record?, &mut ops)?;
+    }
+
+    // Only now: records are grouped by shape rather than ordered by id, so the
+    // id space is legitimately fragmented partway through a buffer and only has
+    // to be whole at the end. A buffer that fails earlier never reaches this,
+    // which is right — it has not finished building the thing being checked.
+    ops.nodes
+        .verify(g.node_id_bound())
+        .map_err(|e| id_space_error_map("node", e))?;
+    ops.edges
+        .verify(g.relationship_id_bound())
+        .map_err(|e| id_space_error_map("relationship", e))?;
+
+    g.commit_index(&mut ops.docs.node_adds, &mut ops.docs.node_removes);
+    g.commit_edge_index(&mut ops.docs.edge_adds, &mut ops.docs.edge_removes);
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+/// A refusal from a bulk node operation, as the divergence it is.
+///
+/// Two arms, and only one of them is really the graph's: whatever it reported
+/// while doing the work. Every judgement about liveness belongs to
+/// [`IdSpace`] — it decides, and its refusals arrive wrapped, to be unwrapped
+/// straight back into the rendering [`id_space_error_map`] gives them.
+fn node_op(
+    kind: &'static str,
+    e: NodeOpError,
+) -> ApplyError {
+    match e {
+        NodeOpError::Graph(e) => ApplyError::Graph(e),
+        NodeOpError::IdSpace(e) => id_space_error_map(kind, e),
+    }
+}
+
+/// A refusal from the id-space check, as the divergence it is.
+///
+/// The graph states these in its own terms — it knows nothing of buffers or of a
+/// peer engine — so the wording that names both sides is added here, where there
+/// is a peer to name.
+fn id_space_error_map(
+    kind: &'static str,
+    e: IdSpaceError,
+) -> ApplyError {
+    match e {
+        IdSpaceError::AlreadyLive { id, entry_bound } => ApplyError::AlreadyLive {
+            kind,
+            id,
+            first_unallocated: entry_bound,
+        },
+        IdSpaceError::AlreadyRecycled(id) => ApplyError::NotLive {
+            kind,
+            id,
+            reason: "it is already in the recycle bin",
+        },
+        IdSpaceError::NeverCreated(id) => ApplyError::NotLive {
+            kind,
+            id,
+            reason: "it was never allocated here",
+        },
+        IdSpaceError::Hole {
+            entry_bound,
+            highest,
+            created,
+        } => ApplyError::IdsHaveAHole {
+            kind,
+            entry_bound,
+            highest,
+            created,
+        },
+        IdSpaceError::Miscounted {
+            graph_bound,
+            expected,
+        } => ApplyError::CountMiscounted {
+            kind,
+            graph_bound,
+            expected,
+        },
+        IdSpaceError::IdOutOfRange(id) => ApplyError::IdPastEndOfSpace { kind, id },
+    }
+}
+
+fn apply_record(
+    g: &mut Graph,
+    record: Record,
+    ops: &mut BufferOps,
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    match record {
+        // One opcode, two variants: the wire's `SchemaType` byte is now the

+            // this name's. That got it wrong in both directions — it accepted a
+            // buffer whose id belonged to a different attribute, which is exactly
+            // the wrong-attribute corruption `IdMismatch` exists to catch, and it
+            // rejected correct buffers whose name was already registered.

+            // dictionary is full, because `ATTRIBUTE_ID_NONE` is reserved out of

+                assigned as i64,

+            ids,
+            labels,
+            attr_ids,
+            rows,
+        } => {

+            // attributes the check is what says `rows` must also be empty —
+            // `rows.len() != ids.len() * 0` — so gating it lets a record
+            // carrying values under an empty `AttrSet` apply silently and drop
+            // them. `UpdateNode` has always checked unconditionally; this is the
+            // same record shape reaching the two paths differently.

+                    &label_ids,
+                    &attr_ids,
+                    &rows,

+        Record::CreateEdge {
+            ids,
+            relation_id,
+            src,
+            dst,
+            attr_ids,

+                dst.iter().collect(),

+        Record::UpdateNode {

+            // row-major entry point so far.
+            let map = attr_map(g, &ids, &attr_ids, &rows)?;

+        Record::SetLabels { ids, labels } => {

+            // `Vec<u64>` first, and a delete-by-label arrives as a consecutive
+            // range — the one shape that has no vector to hand over.
+            let nodes = ids.to_roaring();
+            // Two ways a delete can name something that is not live, and the
+            // graph answers one of them by itself: an id already in the recycle
+            // bin. The other — at or above the boundary this buffer started from
+            // and never created by it, so nothing has ever held it — needs the
+            // batch, which is why it is handed over here.
+            g.delete_nodes(&nodes, &mut ops.docs.node_removes, Some(&ops.nodes))
+                .map_err(|e| node_op("node", e))?;
+            Ok(())
+        }
+
+        Record::DeleteEdge { ids, .. } => {
+            let edges = ids.to_roaring();
+            g.delete_relationships(&edges, &mut ops.docs.edge_removes, Some(&ops.edges))
+                .map_err(|e| node_op("relationship", e))?;
+            Ok(())
+        }

+        Record::CreateIndex {
+            schema_type,
+            label_id,
+            label,
+            field_type,
+            fields,
+            options,
+        } => {
+            verify_schema(g, schema_type, label_id, &label)?;
+            for field in &fields {
+                verify_attribute(g, field.id, &field.name)?;
+            }
+            let index_type = index_type_of(field_type);
+            let label = Arc::new(label);
+            let fields: Vec<Arc<String>> = fields.into_iter().map(|f| Arc::new(f.name)).collect();
+            // Population is spawned, not run here. `populate_indexes_sync` ran
+            // on the Redis main thread, so a replica applying an index over a
+            // large label froze for the whole build — the same class of problem
+            // as expanding ids while decoding.
+            //
+            // Spawning is safe for the reason it is safe on the primary, which
+            // has always done it under concurrent writes: `populate_index_batch`
+            // populates from a snapshot in 10,000-row batches, and entities
+            // written *after* the snapshot are indexed by the write path instead
+            // (`BufferOps::docs` into `commit_index`). A later record that drops
+            // or recreates the index does not race it either — the population
+            // ticket carries a generation, and a worker whose generation is
+            // stale releases its ticket and stops rather than committing
+            // documents into the new spec.
+            g.create_index(
+                &index_type,
+                &schema_type,
+                &label,
+                &fields,
+                index_options(&index_type, &options),
+            )?;
+            Ok(())
+        }
+
+        Record::DropIndex {
+            schema_type,
+            label_id,
+            label,
+            field_type,
+            fields,
+        } => {
+            verify_schema(g, schema_type, label_id, &label)?;
+            for field in &fields {
+                verify_attribute(g, field.id, &field.name)?;
+            }
+            let index_type = index_type_of(field_type);
+            let label = Arc::new(label);
+            let fields: Vec<Arc<String>> = fields.into_iter().map(|f| Arc::new(f.name)).collect();
+            g.drop_index(&index_type, &schema_type, &label, &fields)?;
+            Ok(())
+        }
+
+        Record::CreateConstraint {
+            constraint_type,
+            entity_type,
+            status,
+            label_id,
+            label,
+            props,
+        } => {
+            verify_schema(g, entity_type, label_id, &label)?;
+            for AttrRef { id, name } in &props {
+                verify_attribute(g, *id, name)?;
+            }
+            let properties: Vec<Arc<String>> =
+                props.into_iter().map(|p| Arc::new(p.name)).collect();
+            // Install the master's outcome rather than re-deriving it. A replica
+            // that validated independently would scan at a different time
+            // against different interleavings, and could legitimately reach a
+            // different status. The upsert is what lets the second announcement
+            // — the one carrying the validated status — land on the constraint
+            // the first one created.
+            //
+            // `status` is no longer an `Option` to unwrap: a create carries one
+            // and a drop has no field for it, so the variant settles it.
+            g.upsert_constraint_raw(
+                constraint_type,
+                entity_type,
+                &Arc::new(label),
+                &properties,
+                status,
+            );
+            Ok(())
+        }
+
+        Record::DropConstraint {
+            constraint_type,
+            entity_type,
+            label_id,
+            label,
+            props,
+        } => {
+            verify_schema(g, entity_type, label_id, &label)?;
+            for AttrRef { id, name } in &props {
+                verify_attribute(g, *id, name)?;
+            }
+            let properties: Vec<Arc<String>> =
+                props.into_iter().map(|p| Arc::new(p.name)).collect();
+            g.drop_constraint(&constraint_type, &entity_type, &label, &properties)?;
+            Ok(())
+        }
+    }
+}

+/// `ADD_SCHEMA`: register the label or type, then check the id matches.
+fn apply_add_schema(
+    g: &mut Graph,
+    schema_type: EntityType,
+    id: u32,
+    name: &str,
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    match schema_type {
+        EntityType::Node => {
+            let assigned = usize::from(g.get_label_id_mut(name)) as i64;
+            let local = g.get_labels().get(id as usize).map(|l| l.to_string());
+            verify_id("label", name, i64::from(id), assigned, local)
+        }
+        EntityType::Relationship => {
+            let assigned = g.get_type_id_mut(name).0 as i64;
+            let local = g.get_types().get(id as usize).map(|t| t.to_string());
+            verify_id("relationship type", name, i64::from(id), assigned, local)
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+fn verify_id(
+    kind: &'static str,
+    name: &str,
+    expected: i64,
+    assigned: i64,
+    local: Option<String>,
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    if assigned == expected {
+        return Ok(());
+    }
+    Err(ApplyError::IdMismatch {
+        kind,
+        name: name.to_string(),
+        expected,
+        assigned,
+        local: LocalName(local),
+    })
+}
+
+/// Resolve a label or type by id and confirm the name matches.
+///
+/// The id is authoritative; the name is the cheap cross-check that surfaces
+/// divergence instead of writing through a stale id. Mirrors C's `VerifySchema`.
+fn verify_schema(
+    g: &Graph,
+    schema_type: EntityType,
+    id: u32,
+    name: &str,
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    let (kind, local) = match schema_type {
+        EntityType::Node => (
+            "label",
+            g.get_labels().get(id as usize).map(|l| l.to_string()),
+        ),
+        EntityType::Relationship => (
+            "relationship type",
+            g.get_types().get(id as usize).map(|t| t.to_string()),
+        ),
+    };
+    resolved(kind, name, i64::from(id), local)
+}
+
+/// Mirrors C's `VerifyAttribute`.
+fn verify_attribute(
+    g: &Graph,
+    id: u16,
+    name: &str,
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    let local = g
+        .get_node_attribute_names()
+        .get(id as usize)
+        .map(|a| a.as_str().to_string());
+    resolved("attribute", name, i64::from(id), local)
+}
+
+fn resolved(
+    kind: &'static str,
+    name: &str,
+    id: i64,
+    local: Option<String>,
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    match local {
+        Some(local) if local == name => Ok(()),
+        Some(local) => Err(ApplyError::NameMismatch {
+            kind,
+            name: name.to_string(),
+            id,
+            local,
+        }),
+        None => Err(ApplyError::Unresolved {
+            kind,
+            name: name.to_string(),
+            id,
+        }),
+    }
+}
+
+fn resolve_type(
+    g: &Graph,
+    relation_id: u32,
+) -> Result<Arc<String>, ApplyError> {
+    g.get_type(TypeId(relation_id as usize))
+        .ok_or(ApplyError::IdOutOfRange {
+            kind: "relationship type",
+            id: i64::from(relation_id),
+        })
+}
+
+/// An `UPDATE_EDGE`'s relationship type, checked against this graph.
+///
+/// The same check C's `ApplyUpdateEdge` makes — after reading the record, it
+/// refuses one whose `r_id` is negative or past the local edge-schema count,
+/// logging "references relationship type %d which doesn't exist locally"
+/// (`src/effects/update_edge_effect.c`). A replica that has not
+/// seen the `ADD_SCHEMA` yet must fail here rather than index the rows under a
+/// type it invented.
+///
+/// Takes a bare `u32`: `UpdateEdge` carries a relationship type and `UpdateNode`
+/// has no field for one, so "an edge update with no type" is no longer a state
+/// this can be handed. The `MissingRelType` error that reported it has been
+/// deleted rather than left unconstructible.
+fn checked_type_id(
+    g: &Graph,
+    relation_id: u32,
+) -> Result<TypeId, ApplyError> {
+    resolve_type(g, relation_id)?;
+    Ok(TypeId(relation_id as usize))
+}
+
+/// Expand `(ids, labels)` into the row/column pairs the bulk label API takes,
+/// bounds-checking every label id on the way.
+/// The label ids, checked against this graph's dictionary.
+///
+/// Returns the ids themselves rather than the `ids x labels` product: the
+/// product is `set_node_labels_product`'s to walk lazily, and materializing it
+/// here cost two allocations the size of the product for a caller that then
+/// regrouped it straight back.
+fn checked_label_ids(
+    g: &Graph,
+    labels: &[u32],
+) -> Result<Vec<u64>, ApplyError> {
+    let bound = g.get_labels().len();
+    labels
+        .iter()
+        .map(|&label| {
+            // No `< 0` arm: the wire field is unsigned, so a sentinel cannot
+            // arrive as one. A peer that wrote C's -1 into these four bytes
+            // arrives here as 4294967295 and fails the same bound, which
+            // `IdOutOfRange` renders both ways.
+            if label as usize >= bound {
+                return Err(ApplyError::IdOutOfRange {
+                    kind: "label",
+                    id: i64::from(label),
+                });
+            }
+            Ok(u64::from(label))
+        })
+        .collect()
+}
+
+/// Turn a record's shape plus its row-major values back into per-entity
+/// attribute lists.
+///
+/// A `T_NULL` slot means the property is absent for that entity, which is
+/// unambiguous because FalkorDB never stores a null property value.
+/// Every attribute id resolves here, and the value block is the size the
+/// record's count and shape imply.
+fn check_attr_shape(
+    g: &Graph,
+    ids: &[u64],
+    attr_ids: &[u16],
+    rows: &[Value],
+) -> Result<(), ApplyError> {
+    let bound = g.get_node_attribute_names().len();
+    for &attr_id in attr_ids {
+        if attr_id as usize >= bound {
+            return Err(ApplyError::IdOutOfRange {
+                kind: "attribute",
+                id: i64::from(attr_id),
+            });
+        }
+    }
+    // Strictly ascending, and this is the only place it is enforced.
+    // `insert_attrs_rows` documents the requirement and checks it with a
+    // `debug_assert`, so in a release build an out-of-order `AttrSet` becomes an
+    // unsorted span in the store, and every later property read binary-searches
+    // it: wrong values or a spurious `Null`, compounding on each merge. A
+    // duplicate id puts two entries under one key in the same span.
+    //
+    // No Rust primary emits one — `Pending` keeps a sorted vec — but v3 exists so
+    // that a *C* primary can write these buffers, and C's `AttributeSet` carries
+    // no such guarantee: `AttributeSet_Add` appends, and `AttributeSet_Contains`
+    // finds a key by scanning the ids linearly, under a standing
+    // `// TODO: use SIMD or support sort` (`src/graph/entities/attribute_set.c`).
+    if let Some(w) = attr_ids.windows(2).find(|w| w[0] >= w[1]) {
+        return Err(ApplyError::AttrIdsNotAscending {
+            first: w[0],
+            second: w[1],
+        });
+    }
+    let width = attr_ids.len();
+    if rows.len() != ids.len() * width {
+        return Err(ApplyError::ShapeMismatch {
+            entities: ids.len(),
+            width,
+            values: rows.len(),
+        });
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+fn attr_map(
+    g: &Graph,
+    ids: &[u64],
+    attr_ids: &[u16],
+    rows: &[Value],
+) -> Result<FxHashMap<u64, Vec<(u16, Value)>>, ApplyError> {
+    check_attr_shape(g, ids, attr_ids, rows)?;
+    let width = attr_ids.len();
+
+    let mut map = FxHashMap::default();
+    for (row, &id) in ids.iter().enumerate() {
+        // Nulls are kept, not filtered: a null means "remove this attribute",
+        // and `merge_span` is what removes it. Dropping them here made
+        // `SET x = NULL` a no-op on the replica while the primary removed the
+        // property, so the two diverged silently until the next resync.
+        let pairs: Vec<(u16, Value)> = attr_ids
+            .iter()
+            .enumerate()
+            .map(|(col, &attr_id)| (attr_id, rows[row * width + col].clone()))
+            .collect();
+        // No sort: `check_attr_shape` above has already refused anything that is
+        // not strictly ascending, and the pairs are built in `attr_ids` order.
+        map.insert(id, pairs);
+    }
+    Ok(map)
+}
+/// The record's option block as the engine's own option type.
+///
+/// Almost nothing left to do: `21f37287d` made the record carry
+/// `TextIndexOptions` and `VectorIndexOptions` themselves, so this picks the
+/// half the field type calls for instead of rebuilding it field by field.
+///
+/// What went with the conversion is worth naming, because it was not just
+/// copying. It checked a `dimension` that no longer needs checking — both sides
+/// hold a `u64` now — and it mapped a similarity function through a string
+/// match and a phonetic flag through a `bool`, which was the one narrow
+/// representation in the chain and silently rewrote any algorithm other than
+/// Double Metaphone English. A conversion that cannot happen cannot be wrong.
+///
+/// Absence still survives: every option carries its own presence byte, so
+/// "no language given" and "language english" stay different instructions —
+/// which matters because an effect adds a field to an index that may already
+/// exist, and a language already set for the label refuses a second one.
+fn index_options(
+    index_type: &IndexType,
+    options: &IndexFieldOptions,
+) -> Option<IndexOptions> {
+    match index_type {
+        IndexType::Vector => options.vector.clone().map(IndexOptions::Vector),
+        IndexType::Fulltext => Some(IndexOptions::Text(options.text.clone())),
+        // A range index takes none of these.
+        IndexType::Range => None,
+    }
+}
+
+/// `IndexFieldType` is a bit flag set, so this tests bits rather than matching
+/// a discriminant. Anything that is neither full-text nor vector is a range
+/// index — `INDEX_FLD_RANGE` is itself the union of the three scalar kinds.
+fn index_type_of(field_type: u32) -> IndexType {
+    if field_type & INDEX_FLD_FULLTEXT != 0 {
+        IndexType::Fulltext
+    } else if field_type & INDEX_FLD_VECTOR != 0 {
+        IndexType::Vector
+    } else {
+        IndexType::Range
+    }
+}
